title: Five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–14)
hookLine: a boy hands over his lunch and five thousand are fed
carry: what you hand over is enough

cards: A hillside by the Sea of Galilee, near Passover, with much grass in the place, John says. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out here, thousands of people, a long way from any town. It's getting late.
Everybody's hungry. Jesus turns to Philip, one of his disciples, and asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?"

John adds that he asked this to test him, because he already knew what he would do. Philip counts the cost. Two hundred pence worth of bread, he says, wouldn't be enough for each of them to get a little.
The need is enormous, and what they've got is nothing.

teach.b: Then Andrew speaks up, honest and a little embarrassed: "There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?"
John is the one who tells us it was a boy, and that the loaves were barley.
Some readers note that barley bread was plain, everyday bread. This is a kid's packed lunch, and not a fancy one. Jesus says: make the people sit down.
There's a lot of grass there, and the men sit down, about five thousand of them. Then Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants.
The Greek word for gave thanks is the root of a word Catholics know well: Eucharist.
John's chapter six goes on, the next day, to Jesus calling himself the bread of life, and the Church reads this hillside meal as pointing toward the Mass. Then a detail that's easy to miss.
When everyone's full, Jesus says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost."
They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Nothing wasted, and more left over than they started with.

teach.h: BUT WHAT ARE THESE AMONG SO MANY?
teach.b: In John's telling, it starts with a child who handed over what he had, even though everyone could see it wasn't enough.

how: Catholics read John 6 over several summer Sundays in the year of Mark, from the feeding on the hillside through the bread of life discourse, and hear it as pointing to the Eucharist.

o: from the Hebrew for a Sabbath candle
from the Latin for a holy meal
from the Greek for giving thanks

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

found a boy with a lunch
what the boy's five loaves were

s: Philip has a plan to buy enough bread
he counts the cost: two hundred pence worth wouldn't be enough.
Jesus gives thanks before the bread is handed out
the Greek word for it is the root of Eucharist.
Jesus lets the leftovers go to waste
“Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost.” twelve baskets.

games.q: you're Andrew. thousands of hungry people, and all you've found is a boy with five loaves and two fish. what do you do?
o: bring it to Jesus, even though it isn't enough.
tell everyone to go home and find their own food.
games.why: he brings it: “but what are these among so many?” Jesus gives thanks, and five thousand eat, with twelve baskets left.

practice: Think of a need that seems too big, a friend's grief, a neighbor's struggle, a cause you care about, and of what you actually have. Not much: ten minutes, twenty dollars, one skill, a listening ear, five loaves and two fish.
Choose one small thing you think won't matter and picture handing it over anyway; if you pray, you can offer it to God and let him do the rest.

wordCard.voice: Eucharist. The thanksgiving behind a boy's five loaves and two fish, feeding thousands with baskets of bread left over.

orig.note: Greek: having given thanks. The root of the word Eucharist.

carryVoice: Your line: what you hand over is enough. Twelve baskets, from one small lunch. Day fifty, done.
